The Sorting

Burst Monitor · the read from the Friday, October 16 close

The Sorting

The S&P 500 lost 2% this week while its typical stock gained 2.6% — one of the six widest five-session gaps between the index and its median name since 2000, and the third this year. Ten companies made the loss; every other sector rose at the median. The river drew the week as two groups that held their membership for three sessions and went opposite ways in price: an AI-hardware core down 7%, a block of financials and industrials still ten points below August up 1%, the other 384 names up 3%. The ten largest companies rolled down their own cycles together while the field crested behind them. The coordination on the board is the sorting. It is not yet a swing.

Where we left off · one edition, two logs, one repair

Tuesday, Oct 13
The Crest Travels. The index had made a record on October 6 without the typical stock, and then five shared crests had traveled from the AI-hardware leaders to the utilities and railroads. The ten largest companies shared one phase just past their crest; the field had none. Rotation, measured; repair withheld. The fork: the rotation continues, or the field swings together on the way down.
Wednesday, Oct 14
A day-of log. The shorter memory — the 204-session current that had flipped from anti-coupled to coupled on the day of the record — took the raw book from the 384-session incumbent, which stepped back to 396 to meet it. First print; the settled book needed two more.
Thursday, Oct 15
Two tool corrections and one census. The floor-loss band on Waves had been drawing every episode at one depth; separated, S1 walks across memory lengths, and this month's fire at 378 sessions turned out to be the tooth's narrow lag search reading a secondary peak. The lead/lag cells — coiling, easing, settled, fragile — were named and measured against the record: Jason's rule that a lagging, anti-coupled memory is a fragile place survived a control for price state. The 204 handoff completed on Friday morning's build, on Thursday's observation.
This morning
Sol read first (The Rest Advances While the Index Gives Ground). Jason walked the board and named six things: both story counts turning down, the deep rust under a hot edge on the spectrogram, the recent agreement days, the 60-session tip leading over negative correlation, the dial tipping toward the descending side, and large river blocks holding together for three sessions. Claude read from the data and froze it. Sol reviewed the read and found an error in it — one that turned out to be older than the read, and in the instrument. Chapter 6 is that story. The repair was applied before these stills were taken.

Chapter 1 · October 9 → October 16

The widest week but five

From Friday to Friday the S&P 500 fell 1.95%, from 7,811.54 to 7,659.44. The median of its 501 current members rose 2.57%, and 70% of them were higher. The equal-weight average rose 0.71%. The typical stock beat the index by 4.5 points in five sessions. On this roster's record since 2000 only five sessions were wider: April 14, 2000 (+6.6, the April 2000 crash), December 21, 2000 (+5.4), July 29 of this year (+4.8), July 17, 2024 (+4.8, the week the "great rotation" out of megacap technology was named), and June 10 of this year (+4.6). Friday is sixth. The exact combination of this week — index down more than 1.5%, median up more than 2% — has happened twice before, both this summer: June 26 and July 29.

The index's loss belongs to ten companies. The ten largest by market value, 38.9% of the index, contributed −1.46 of the −1.93 points the roster lost on a cap-weighted basis; the other 491 names contributed −0.46 — the net of the rest of Technology (−1.53) and everything outside it (+1.07). By sector the split is cleaner still: Technology, 38% of the index's value, lost 2.9% at the median with 36% of its names up and took 2.43 points off the index; the other ten sectors were all positive at the median and together added 0.50. Staples rose 5.3% at the median with every one of its 32 names up. Energy +5.1%, Healthcare +3.9%, Consumer Cyclicals +3.6%, Utilities +3.1%. Inside the ten: Micron −14.6%, Broadcom −9.1%, Tesla −7.3%, Nvidia −6.6%, Amazon −4.7%, Alphabet −3.1%, Meta −1.3%, Microsoft −1.1%. Apple rose 2.0% and Berkshire 3.2%, and both closed Friday at their 63-session highs. The descending heavies are the AI complex, not the whole top of the index. Below them, most of the week's worst names are the optical and hardware supply chain: Ciena −26%, Coherent −25%, Lumentum −25%, Hewlett Packard Enterprise −25%, Flex −25%, Super Micro −24%, Dell −23%; Paramount Skydance (−25%), Bloom Energy (−21%) and Pinterest (−20%) sit among them.

The three big days were two different markets. On Wednesday the index fell 1.11% on a hot inflation print, the median stock fell 0.08%, and the ten fell 1.97% at their median. On Thursday the index rose 0.33% while the median stock rose 1.47% and 75.6% of names were up — the broadest day in weeks, with the ten at +0.08%, absent from it. On Friday the index fell 1.09%, the median stock fell 0.01%, the ten fell 2.22%. Since the October 6 record the index is −2.04% and the typical stock +2.87%; since August 13 the index is −1.79% and the typical stock −4.13%, with 32% of names higher. The rest has had two weeks of its turn and is still four points behind where August left it.

Who received it

The receivers this week were the defensives and the cyclicals alike: staples, energy, healthcare, consumer cyclicals, utilities, materials. Financials rose 1.9% at the median and the insurance brokers led them — Brown & Brown, Erie, Gallagher — with most of the health insurers up 4–7% after UnitedHealth raised its guidance (Humana −4%). The week's leaders by name are software and services, not hardware: FICO +15.5%, Cognizant +11.5%, Accenture +10.7%, Tyler +9.5%, with Equifax, Darden, ConocoPhillips and Keurig Dr Pepper beside them. Whether the receiving sectors are economically sound — Jason's question, and the right one — is not something the instrument can grade; it can only test whether their crest holds, which is chapter 7's business.

Chapter 2 · the river

Two groups

Jason's eye on the river, before any of this was measured: "that top row to the right — that large group that has moved together for three sessions. Same for the tech-dominated group underneath it. The more I look, the more I see bits of coordination." The river is the Currents view of the market as rooms — communities of names that co-burst over a 63-session window, matched day to day — drawn as ribbons through time. Rooms are rebuilt every morning and their labels are local; what persists is membership. So the test of Jason's eye is to freeze the exact names and follow them.

The Technology-led room was 81 names on Friday. 54 of them were in it on all three of Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, and 51 of those 54 were already together on Tuesday. It holds 22 Technology names, 10 Industrials, 4 Energy, 4 Consumer Cyclicals, and a scattering; it is 25.4% of the index's value. Its median return on the week was −7.11%, with a third of its names up. Since the record, −7.2%. The Financial-Services-led room was 83 names on Friday; 64 were in it all three sessions. It is 24 Financials, 9 Real Estate, 9 Industrials, 8 Healthcare, 6 Cyclicals; 7.2% of the index's value. On Tuesday 56 of those 64 names were in two rooms — 29 in a financials block, 27 in a block led by industrials and real estate — and Wednesday's rebuild put them together. Their median return on the week was +1.07%, two-thirds of them up (63 of the 64 are on the price roster; with Moderna it is +1.05%). Since August 13 they are still −10.5% at the median: the laggards' laggards. The other 384 names on the roster: +3.13% on the week, 76% up.

So the two blocks Jason saw holding together are the two sides of the week. The one that lost is the AI complex plus its industrial suppliers; the one that gained, a little, is the block that had lost the most since August. Co-residence matched the sign of the week's return in both. That is more than "those ribbons look organized": it is a room's membership predicting, for one week, which way its members went. One week.

Bits of coordination, counted

The river has a number for what Jason saw. A moving group is a set of names whose room sequence over the last five sessions is identical and includes at least one move between rooms — an exact-route class, no clustering, no tolerance. The share of names in such groups of five or more is the river's coherence line. On Wednesday it printed 45.6%, the highest value in the 45-session window; Thursday 44.4%, the second highest; Friday 41.8%, fourth, behind October 5. The window's median is 27.5% and its low was 8.4% on September 4. The number of rooms went 11 → 10 → 8 → 9 → 9 across the week, with four deaths on Wednesday and none on Friday; the day-over-day identity of the rooms (median matched Jaccard) rose from 0.50 on Monday to 0.79 on Friday. Reorganization early in the week, then a still endpoint.

Two cautions, both Sol's. Similar weekly returns, shared rooms, and synchronized phase are three different observations, not one. The 54-name core's cap-weighted phase hand is coherent (R 0.73 at 0.43 of a cycle, descending toward its trough) but its equal-weight hand is a zero (R 0.30): its heavy members share a phase, its many light members do not. And the moving-group layer is a finder — exact-route classes restate on every rebuild. "Sorting into persistent groups" is the sentence the evidence carries; "each half moving together" is one step past it.

Chapter 3 · the dial

The ten rolled

The Phase Dial reads each stock's position in its own twenty-session rhythm — 0 at the crest, 0.5 at the trough — and draws the roster as a ring, with two hands for the mean phase: one counting every name equally, one weighting each by its market value. A hand with R below 0.35 is a zero: it has no usable direction. On Friday both market hands are zeros — count R 0.325, weight R 0.267. A week ago the count hand was 0.40 on the rising flank and the weight hand 0.30; neither has been above the lock line of 0.55 since September 9. The split hands tell the story the whole hands cannot.

The ten largest companies share one phase at R 0.73, 0.40 of a cycle past their crest: descending, nearly at the trough. A week ago they were at 0.13, just past home, as The Crest Travels left them. Nvidia went 0.22 → 0.51, Broadcom 0.17 → 0.53, Micron 0.26 → 0.54, Tesla 0.06 → 0.49: four of the ten have reached the bottom of their own cycle. Amazon, Alphabet and Meta are at 0.35–0.39, descending. Apple is at 0.16 and Microsoft at 0.21, still near home. The spread is why R is 0.73 and not 0.92. The other 491 names: R 0.34 at 0.05, a zero sitting at home — because Thursday was their crest. By count, 51% of the roster is in the first quarter past the crest, 9% in the descending quarter, 22% just past the trough, 18% rising. Jason's "tipping to the downward flank" is right about the direction of travel — a week ago the two right-hand quarters held 28% of names and now hold 60% — but the descending quarter itself is nearly empty. Friday's face is "half the field crested on Thursday, the ten are at their trough."

What the record says about this shape, with the mask on

The shape on the dial is: the ten coherent (R at least 0.6) and descending (ψ between 0.3 and 0.5) while the other 491 are a zero (R below 0.35). On today's roster, with episodes five sessions apart and the last sixty-three sessions excluded, the record has 58 of them. Over the next twenty sessions the index's median move was +0.9% with 64% up, against +1.3% and 64% at the base rate; over sixty-three sessions +2.3% against +3.3%. The ten themselves ran −0.9% over the next twenty sessions against +2.3% at base: on this shape the heavy names kept lagging the field for a month. The median stock did what it always does, +1.6%. And the field went on to lock — the count hand rising through 0.55 — within ten sessions in 41% of the cases against 57% at base; with the index within 5% of its high, as it is now, in only 24% of seventeen cases. After this shape the field tends to stay dispersed. The left tail is real: the tenth-percentile worst path over sixty-three sessions is −15.8% against −13.6%, and the list of dates includes July 19 and 26, 2024, February 21 and 28, 2025, and December 16, 2021 — each a few weeks before a slide. The conditions were written after seeing the shape; the ten are today's ten by today's values, so survivorship is heavy; the windows overlap.

The branch the first read called "everything swings" was not defined properly the first time — it required the rest to be coherent but said nothing about where — and Sol caught it. Defined properly, the swing is the rest coherent and within 0.15 of a cycle of the ten's position: 86 cases, next-ten median −1.5%, next-twenty −0.9% with 47% up, and a tenth-percentile worst path over sixty-three sessions of −24%. Tighter still, the rest coherent and itself descending: 69 cases, −2.5% and −1.2%, 39% up. Those are 2022's dates, with May and September 2021, September 2023 and April 2025 among them. The record sorts the fork by one thing: whether the other 491 lock while the ten descend. They have not.

The sectors, and the trough

By sector the hands are where the crest left them: Utilities R 0.87 at 0.04, Energy 0.75 at 0.06, Staples 0.74 at 0.07, Healthcare 0.72 at 0.12 — all just past home, all coherent. Financials R 0.31 at 0.93, Real Estate 0.50 at 0.89: rising into it. Technology R 0.29 at 0.39: dispersed and descending, its 85 names split 26 / 23 / 28 / 8 across the quarters. Industrials R 0.15: no phase at all. The 64-name block of chapter 2 has a hand of its own — R 0.52 at 0.78, rising, from 0.72 at 0.63 a week ago: it passed its own trough in the first week of October and is climbing toward its crest. The 54-name block by count is a zero at 0.46; by weight, 0.73 at 0.43.

One more number about the ten. On the record, when their hand sits at 0.35–0.45 of a cycle with R of 0.6 or better — 89 cases — it reached the trough within twenty sessions in 74 of them, a median two sessions later, with the index about −2% and the ten about −3% on the way. Fifteen never got there inside the window. The ten will most likely be at the bottom of their cycle by mid-week. That dates the rhythm. It does not date the low; the guide's rule, measured on the October 13 locks, is that the phase runs ahead of price.

Chapter 4 · the crests

Five in a row, two that vanished

A closure fires when at least 8% of the pool — 59 of 748 names — are at the crest of their own twenty-session rhythm on the same day. In today's reconstruction every session this week was one: October 12 (74 closers), 13 (77), 14 (103), 15 (140), 16 (71). Thursday's 140 is 18.7% of the pool, 2.4 times the line, the 76th percentile of closure-day shares since 2000 (the 85th of all sessions') and nowhere near the record's top (the May 2025 recovery crested 250–290 names a day). Five closures in a row is ordinary: 198 such runs in the record, and the index afterward did what it does at base. The shape is in who crested, and in what the ledger did to last week's story.

The cast traveled again, inside the week. Take each day's closers on the roster and ask how they had done against the index from August 13 to October 9. Monday's 44 closers were 3.5 points ahead of the index — the rest's leaders — with 12.8% of the index's value; Tuesday's 51 were 3.8 ahead; Wednesday's 81 were even (−0.3), Healthcare 16 and Utilities 16, 14.3% of value; Thursday's 105 were even, Healthcare 23 and Staples 16, 15.4% of value; Friday's 50 were 9.3 points behind, Utilities 11 and Financials 8, 3.7% of the index's value. Leaders of the rest first, the middle of the field midweek, the deepest laggards last. Of the ten, only Alphabet's two lines crested, on Monday; none after that.

What the ledger did to last week's crests

The Crest Travels reported five crests in seven sessions: October 2, 5, 6, 9 and 12. Today's ledger has October 2 (74) and 5 (63), then no closure on October 6 (57 of 59), 7, 8 or 9 (49 of 59), then the five of this week. October 6 and October 9 are dropped. October 9 is the instructive one: it printed exactly at the line on its first morning, below it the next, then 77, 79, 70, 69 across four builds — the October 14 log called it "confirmed and raised" — and then 49 on the October 17 build. October 6 held for five builds at 70, 69, 72, 63, 63 and fell to 57 on the October 16 build. The guide's rule from last week, that a closure becomes a fact on the build after the next close, was wrong, and it was wrong in a way the record now measures.

How far back the ledger restates, measured

Eighteen morning builds from September 23 to October 17 (the two contaminated October 5–6 runs excluded), each compared with today's ledger session by session: the newest session printed low, by 12.8 names on average, 83% of the time, by as much as 38. The one to four sessions behind the newest printed high, by 5 to 8 on average, by as much as 30. At seven sessions behind the mean absolute revision was 3.3 names and the largest 9. No fired flag changed more than six sessions behind the edge in these eighteen builds, against today's reconstruction — which is itself a vintage that will restate. Counts and classifications are different objects: a count is still moving a handful of names a week later; a classification, in this sample, had settled by six sessions. For this week that means October 12 and 13, four and three sessions back with margins of +15 and +18, have probably settled; October 14 (+44), 15 (+81) and 16 (+12) are in the band that moves. The audit's pattern says what to expect on Tuesday's build — a low first print rising, a high second print falling — and nothing about by how much.

The map: this week's arrow is data

The motion map's compass — the mean of every name's five-session displacement — reads R 0.73 at −96°, drift 0.21 at the one-year lens: a coherent push straight down, into pressure. Last week most of the six-month lens's arrow was the April release leaving its window. This week the standing check says the opposite: holding the window where it stood on October 9 and appending the five new sessions reproduces the arrow almost exactly (R 0.74, drift 0.21 at 252; 0.82 and 0.30 at 126), and the exit alone is drift 0.01 at the year lens and 0.04 at the half-year. The dives are real. 126 names went through the floor, 3 came back up, and the divers were the winners — median +4.4% on the week, spread across Financials 18, Healthcare 18, Cyclicals 16, Utilities 15, Staples 13 — because a dive is a crest seen from the pressure side. 214 of 501 are below the floor now. Of the fifteen largest companies only Microsoft, Berkshire, Lilly and Walmart are among them. The AI heavies are quiet by pressure while they fall in price: the instrument's way of saying their move is their own, not a shared burst.

Chapter 5 · the memory

The books and the short end

Four of Jason's six observations were about the whole-market readers: the story counts falling, the spectrogram's deep rust under a hot edge, the agreement days, and the short memory leading over negative correlation. Each is a real observation. Each is also an edge print of a transform that restates, and the guide's job is to say which part of the observation is the market and which is the edge. Here they are in that order, with the handoff that completed on Thursday at the end.

The story counts

The story count is the effective number of independent directions in the names' returns over 21 and 63 sessions; a storm is when it falls below 55% of its trailing-year median. On Friday both fell: PR21 from 13.28 to 12.11, PR63 from 20.46 to 19.37. Those are large one-day drops — in the bottom 2% and 3% of daily changes on the two series — and Jason saw them. Two qualifications. PR63 at 19.4 is at the 93rd percentile of its whole record and up 2.6 over 21 sessions; the storm line is 9.2, half of today. And Friday's drop retraces Thursday's jump — the broad up day added a full story — so over five sessions PR63 is flat. This is a market telling more separate stories than on 93% of sessions since 2000, with one loud session of consolidation at the end of the week. The direction is recorded; a condition needs more than one session. The strip labeled "the three depths," which rose, is the 21-session correlation of the two counts' daily changes (Sol's correction: two depths, not three), and it rose because both fell on Friday.

The spectrogram, and the edge that comes in hot

The memory spectrogram ranks the names' amplitude disagreement at sixteen memory depths against each depth's own history: blue is loud disagreement, rust is deep agreement. Jason's screen showed rust at the deep rungs on the right edge under his smoothing, and asked what it looks like raw. Raw: on October 7 twelve of the sixteen rungs read in the agreement range (0.16–0.33); on October 8, fourteen rungs read below 0.27 — the locked zero of the amplitude book, seen across every memory. October 12 and 13 re-blued (0.61–0.93 on the 13th). On October 14 and 15 the six deep rungs — 315 to 756 sessions — went back to rust at 0.21–0.30 while the shallowest rungs stayed blue and the middle rungs sat in the interior. On October 16 every one of the sixteen rungs printed above 0.99: the loudest disagreement the ruler can register, the first all-sixteen peg since March 27, 2025. The displayed column, a centered five-session median, shows Wednesday and Thursday's deep rust because at the tip it has only three sessions to work with; Monday and Tuesday's builds will decide what Friday's column becomes.

That the edge comes in hot is not a guess; it is the audit. The amplitude book's as-printed spread has settled lower than its first print on every one of the last ten mornings, by 0.10 to 0.37 (Wednesday: 1.477 printed, 1.152 settled; Thursday: 1.420 → 1.189), extending the 42-of-42 audit of September. Friday's 1.546 — higher than all but eleven of the 6,592 prior settled values, sixteen of sixteen rungs scatter-pegged — will settle. By how much, the archive does not say. The question for Tuesday is whether it settles onto the deep rust of Wednesday and Thursday, and whether the rust then steps toward the 157–252 rungs. Two visits to the deep rungs in seven sessions with the shallow rungs blue is the guide's advancing front from the deep end: a candidate, logged twice before this autumn, once wrong by the following Monday.

The agreement days

The fixed amplitude book printed locked zeros — agreement among the names' amplitude states below the trailing-year floor — on September 10, 14, 15, 16 and 17, and on October 7 and 8. October 7 is new: it was apart in last week's reconstruction and is 1.113 against a floor of 1.119 in this one. Jason's question was what kind of climate admits them. The count does not answer it: seven in the trailing 63 sessions against 6.7 expected by the construction (10.7% of all days are zeros), the 62nd percentile of the trailing count, with the record's median at 3 and its 75th percentile at 11. The placement is the thing the construction was tested on, and the placement here is two days at the record close and five in the September drift. What would make the climate question sharper is the pair Sol named: agreement days recurring while the story count is falling. The story count is at its 93rd percentile. Not yet.

The short end, leading

The sweep correlates the market's burst energy with the depth of its drawdown at every memory length from 60 to 1,500 sessions and at every lag, and keeps the best lag. Jason read the 60-session tip on the Synthesis spectrum as leading over negative correlation, and on the long sweep it is: W60 reads r −0.56 with burst leading by 20 sessions, W72 −0.64 leading by 24 — easing in Thursday's vocabulary, the field moving ahead of a shrinking drawdown. At W84 and W96 the sign is still negative but burst lags by 43 — the geometry of the fragile cell. From 108 to 132 the sign is positive; from 144 to 168 it is negative again and in step (lag −1); from 180 up it is positive and lagging, the 204 current's band. The short end flipped on October 8, the zero day (W60 went +0.34 → −0.37), deepened through Wednesday (−0.57) and held there. None of it is a balance point: the peak detector calls only 204 and 396, and depths below 130 are the sweep's shaded region, so no cell prints and the winner-point census does not transfer. Read as a relationship against the drawdown, the three-month memory says "coordination fell as the drawdown shrank" — the record run was a quiet rally — while the ten-month memory says "coordination rose as the drawdown deepened" — the spring. Two memories, two stories, the short one moving first. A watch.

The handoff, completed

The settled reach moved from 384 to 204 sessions on Thursday's observation, as the October 14 log said it would if two more prints came. Friday is the fourth consecutive raw print: 204 at +0.888, lag −136. The displaced structure sits at 396 at +0.868, lag −165, still coherent, with no active challenge (distance 3 is the ceiling, not a count). The contest table, over the same five sessions for both: 204 gained 0.044 in strength while the deep structure lost 0.015 as its peak slid from the 384 row to the 396 row — the challenger strengthened, the incumbent barely moved. Both are settled cells: positive against the drawdown, burst lagging; burst energy itself is flat, 30.6 to 30.7. The market's memory kept its sign and halved its depth. The legacy floor-loss band still prints S1 at 378 sessions for October 13–16; at the long sweep's neighbors of that window (372 and 384) the structure reads +0.83 and +0.87 at lags of −154 and −166, so the tooth is still reading its secondary negative peak through its ±60 keyhole, as Thursday's review found. Persistence of the band is observed; a floor-loss condition is not.

Chapter 6 · construction

What the instrument learned about itself

Two things this week were about the instrument rather than the market. One is the ledger's restatement, measured in chapter 4. The other is an error, and it is the reason the stills in this edition were taken at 13:19 UTC rather than 10:49.

Erratum · the count hand counted missing names as sitting at home

Sol, reviewing the first read's scripts, found that the market-wide count hand was built as the mean of unit vectors over every name on the roster, with names that had no phase on a session — not yet listed, no price history — entered as vectors at phase zero. The expression was copied from The Crest Travels' analysis, which carried the same error, and the same line is in the production film's own chord. The weighted hand and every subgroup hand mask correctly, and on any session where every name has a phase the error is nil: today's hands are exact. Inside this edition's window three names listed this summer (FDXF, HONA, PSKY) have no phase on some sessions, so the masked and unmasked count hands differ there by at most 0.006 in R — below anything this piece prints. Before 2015 it is not nil. The roster had 353 names with phases in 2001 and 416 in 2010 against 501 now, so the historical count hand carried a phantom crest of 85 to 148 names; its R exceeded 1 on sixteen sessions; its record median was 0.51 and is 0.44; the share of sessions on which it is a zero was 25% and is 32%.

Jason chose to repair it the same morning — "I am the only one using this right now, so still dev time; the point of the tool is to accurately tell a story." Sol applied the one-line mask to both count harmonics in the film and its retained comparator, aligned the map's "a zero" cutoff to the dial's fixed 0.35, rebuilt the film, the history and every episode, training, blind and analog film, and verified: four regression tests, ninety rebuilt film payloads, 313 protected files unchanged. The repaired history matches the corrected research series on all 6,605 sessions to the encoding's rounding. The independent fact-check found one loose end: the Phase Dial reads the film and had not been rebuilt when these stills were taken, so its displayed window still carries the unmasked values — a difference of at most 0.006 in R on the sessions where those three names lack a phase, and nil on Friday. The record tables of The Crest Travels were rerun with the mask. Here is what survived.

What survives: the hand's position at the lock still sorts the record, and at least as sharply as published — a lock just past the crest is 27% up over the next twenty sessions (19–24% with the locks spaced first), a lock just past the trough 90%, the descending flank 16%. What weakens, or may: the tape's sign into the lock reads as a smaller sorter than published under the published construction (episodes spaced within each subset): +1.8% after a tape-down lock against +0.6% after a tape-up lock, not +2.8 against +0.65. The fact-check's variant — spacing applied to all locks first, then split — gives +2.5 to +2.9% against +0.4 to +0.6%, close to the published figures. The sign's sorting power is construction-sensitive; the position's is not (the crest row reads 19–27% up and the trough row 83–92% in every variant tried). What is retracted: the October 13 dial shape was not rare — 156 cases, not 43, because phantom coherence had made "count a zero" look rarer than it is — and its lean is base-like; the "tighter cut" tail note with its 2007, 2020, 2022 and 2025 dates was an artifact of the error and is withdrawn. The sentence from September that the weight hand is a zero about as often as the count is corrected: the count is a zero on 32% of sessions, the weight on 25%. The October 13 edition is preserved as published with an erratum at its head; the guide is at v0.9.5. The first read's own error of the morning — calling this week's gap the widest on record when five were wider — is logged beside it.

Chapter 7 · unresolved

Three ways from here

Last week's fork was rotation against a swing, and the market answered the first week of it: the crest kept traveling, the ten rolled, the field did not lock. Sol's framing for what comes next has three branches rather than two, and this edition describes the first while keeping the other two open. It does not have to resolve the market's next act to tell this week's story accurately.

branch oneThe rotation continues among separate groups

  • The other 491 names stay a zero (count R below 0.35) while the ten reach their trough and sit there.
  • The next closures' casts stay in the rest — small shares of the index's value, not the ten as a group.
  • The 54 and the 64 keep their membership and keep diverging in price; the river's coherence stays high.
  • The story count holds near its high; the spectrogram's rust stays at the deep rungs or fades.
  • On the record of today's shape: the index near base, the ten lagging the field for a month, the field not locking (24% within ten sessions near a high).

branch twoThe groups synchronize in descent

  • The rest's count hand rises through 0.55 while the ten are still descending or at the trough — the swing. Print the ten-session return into the lock and where the hand points.
  • The story count falls over five sessions, not one; the deep rust survives Friday's settle and steps toward 157–252.
  • The 64 crest and fade in price; the other 384 give back Thursday's gains; a closure's cast becomes the ten again.
  • Agreement days recur while the count falls — Sol's pair.
  • On the record of the rest coherent and descending with the ten: −2.5% at ten sessions, 39% up at twenty, a tenth-percentile worst path of −25% over a quarter. 2022's dates.

branch threeThe receivers hold as the heavies recover

  • The ten turn up from their trough (phase 0.5 → 0.75) with Apple and Microsoft still near home, and the index follows them up.
  • The 64's crest holds in price; the median name's gap to August 13 closes from −4.1; the laggards' gains persist after their crest. This is the guide's definition of repair.
  • The 54 bottom in price without the rest giving back its two weeks.
  • The 204 current keeps control and its sign; the short end's negative band fades as the record run leaves the three-month window.
  • No census for this one: it is the branch in which both groups keep what they have, and the record's shape censuses do not condition on it.

Sol's note on the receivers belongs here as well. Energy can benefit from an input-cost shock that damages the wider economy; a health insurer can raise its guidance in the same week an employer survey projects benefit costs rising 8% next year; a defensive sector can receive a rotation without being economically healthy. "Defensive," "receiving," and "sound" are three claims, and the instrument tests only the second. The third is the discussion.

The rotation has continued through a falling index. The heavies have moved farther down their own cycles while much of the field has advanced. Neither fact establishes a broad market breakdown or completed repair.

The system is tipping to the downward flank; it isn't cohered yet, but I would watch that. The more I look at the river, the more I see bits of coordination. The market sorted into two persistent groups and the coordination on the board is the sorting, not yet a swing. The ten rolled; the field crested behind them; the record sorts the fork by whether the other 491 lock. They haven't.

Interpretation

  • A sorted market: two persistent groups, each coherent within itself in return, with no common hand.
  • The coordination Jason saw is the rotation sorting into blocks, not the field converging.
  • The ten's descent is their own cycle; the field's crest is Thursday's.
  • The deep rust is a candidate front; the short end is a watch; the story count's fall is one session.
  • Repair withheld: the laggards' block is still ten points below August.

Not established

  • A direction. The record's shape census is 58 cases with today's ten by today's values, conditions written after the shape, overlapping windows.
  • A mechanism. Inflation, oil and the AI selloff are beside the geometry, not under it.
  • That the deep rust is a front; that the short end's sign means more than what its window contains; that the gap's precedents (two, both this summer) are a template.
  • Any number on the newest two or three ticks of the ledger, the amplitude book or the chord; any room's classes or cores beyond this rebuild.

Glossary, in the order the piece uses it

The typical stock, the median name
The middle of the 501 current S&P 500 members' returns, every name equal. The index is cap-weighted; the gap between the two is the concentration.
Pressure, the floor, a dive
Each stock's participation in the market's shared bursts against its own one-year normal. Below the floor is more than normal. Pressure decays with a 21-session half-life and is refilled only when a name crests, so a dive through the floor is a crest seen from the pressure side.
The river, a room, a core
Currents' communities of names that co-burst over a 63-session window, matched day to day and drawn as ribbons. Labels are local to each rebuild; membership is what persists. A core is the exact set of names present in a room on consecutive sessions, frozen.
A moving group, the coherence line
Names whose room sequence over the last five sessions is identical and includes a move. The coherence line is their share of the partition.
Phase, the crest, the trough
Where a stock sits in its own twenty-session rhythm, as an angle: 0 is the crest (home), 0.25 descending, 0.5 the trough, 0.75 rising.
The count hand, the weight hand, a zero, a lock
The mean phase as a vector, every name equal (count) or weighted by today's market value (weight). R is its length; below 0.35 it is a zero; rising through 0.55 is a lock. The ten's hand and the rest's hand are the same object on subsets.
A closure, the cast
A closure fires when at least 8% of the pool is at the crest on one day. The cast is who: by sector, by share of the index's value, by how those names had done against the index before.
First print, settled, the edge
What a series shows on the morning its newest session arrives, against what it shows after later sessions are appended. The phase-based series restate at the edge: closers low, amplitude high, and the sessions just behind the newest high.
The story count, the storm line
The effective number of independent directions in the names' returns over 21 or 63 sessions. A storm is the 63-session count falling below 55% of its trailing-year median.
The spectrogram, a rung, rust
The names' amplitude disagreement at sixteen memory depths, each ranked against its own trailing history. Rust is deep agreement, blue loud disagreement.
The sweep, a balance point, a cell
The correlation of burst energy with drawdown depth at every memory length and lag. A balance point is a local peak in strength at a depth of 130 or more. A cell names its sign (against the drawdown) and who moves first: coiling, easing, settled, fragile.
The settled reach, the handoff
The five-session median of the strongest balance point's depth. A handoff is a new depth taking it, which 204 did from 384 on Thursday.
THEN / NOW
A saved morning's package (testimony) against today's rebuilt history (reconstruction). A reconstruction is never called an earlier warning; a dropped closure is still testimony about its morning.
